extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of poetics (composers of tragic drama)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragedies (plot, recognition, character, parts, and speech) according to classical poetics: how incidents, recognitions, customs, and diction should be arranged to produce proper tragic effect (pity, fear, recognition, reversal).

rubrics_metrics.name: States of action (status) — knowledge/ignorance/recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions must be judged by whether the agent acts willingly/knowingly, unwillingly/unknowingly, with later recognition, or refrains despite knowing; these states determine moral and tragic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the agent who knows he will act and then recognizes (this avoids turpitude and produces admirable recognition). The worst is one who knows and does not act (the poem is then disgraceful). Ambiguous acting is rare and should be used sparingly (example: Creon/Haemon in Antigone). Examples and contrasts: Euripides' Medea (killing knowingly), Sophocles' Oedipus (recognition after action), Iphigenia/Alexandrian examples of recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis) should be drawn from action
rubrics_metrics.description: The best recognitions are those derived from the things of action themselves rather than from external signs or mere report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for recognitions that arise from onstage action (as in Sophocles' Oedipus and Iphigenia) because these are more admirable and moving. Lesser recognitions include those by analogy, by signs (scars, tokens), or by narrative/letters; these are permissible but less artful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrational or extraneous elements in the play
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational elements should not occur within the substance of a tragedy; what is irrational should be kept outside the poem or be otherwise justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce inexplicable or wildly implausible occurrences as part of the action. External or foreign events may be referred to but should not violate the internal probability and coherence of the plot. If something seems irrational, place it as extra-tragic material or justify it thoroughly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents must conform to custom/probability (consuetudo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events and behaviours in the plot must accord with recognisable customs/traits so the audience perceives them as true; Aristotle gives four kinds of consuetudo by which truth is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use one or more of the four standards of custom: (1) goodness (a custom considered good in the genre), (2) conveniency/fittingness (what suits a given kind of person), (3) similarity (things like those the audience expects from a certain type), and (4) equity/average balance. A custom suitable for men may not suit women, etc. Choose customs appropriate to character and circumstance to make incidents believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external signs/tokens for recognition — permissible but secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions can be effected by prepared signs (tokens, scars, letters), but these are not as artful as recognitions from action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tokens like Gegenes' spear, stars, scars (Odysseus), letters or objects may be used to trigger recognition, but prefer action-based revelations. Reserve token-recognition when action-derived recognition is impossible, and make their use credible (e.g., a known scar, a family token).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on chance or irrelevant accidents for crucial outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Key plot turns should not come from mere chance or events irrelevant to the poem's nature; they should follow from the plot's own necessities or customs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making the plot hinge on accidental or extraneous events unless those events are integrated into the poem's world and justified (for example, only use foreign or external incidents at margins or for framing, not as core machinery). Examples in the text warn against conversions that change the nature of the action (e.g., inappropriate shifts of cause).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of tragedy: ligatio (complication) and solutio (resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy is composed of parts including complication (ligation) and resolution (solutio); transitions should move from the one toward the other producing reversal or outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct ligation as what precedes the transition to fortune/infortune; solutio is the progression from that transition to the end. Ensure that the capture of plot elements and their resolutions follow naturally (example: Theodectes' Lyceum example of ligation and later solutio in the capture and fate of an infant). Organize transitions so the audience sees the necessity of the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species of tragedy and consistency of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four species of tragedy; composition must remain consistent to the chosen species, and parts (e.g., recognitions, circumvolutions) must cohere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the properties of the species you adopt (composed, circumvolution with recognition, passive, Tartarus/temporal-testing types) and do not mix incompatible species or structures. If a tragedy is composed in one species, both its composition and resolution should align; poets who mix species risk coherence failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epic/epopoeic treatment in tragedy (appropriate magnitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should not be made into an epic in meter or scope; parts take on length and magnitude appropriate to tragic effect, not the extended narrative of an epic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use epopoeic abundance of meter that belongs to long epics (e.g., an Iliad-like scale) within a tragedy. Keep episodes to lengths and magnitudes that suit stage performance and the unity of action; avoid sprawling narratives that break tragic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke proper emotions (pity, fear, anger) with suitable forms and probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots and scenes should be arranged to elicit pity, fear, anger or similar passions; use forms and figures that fit the probable to make these emotions convincing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare scenes (figures and forms) so they provoke the intended passions: vivid pain, terror, anger, or the perception of magnitude/smallness. Use probable causes for these emotions (a wise man deceived, the unjust triumphing over the strong, etc.) rather than impossible situations. Chorus and style must serve this emotional effect (e.g., chorus in Tartarus for hypocrites).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering of action and speech — demonstrate and prepare passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters of invention and arrangement should make actions visible and prepare the audience for the passions; parts of the poem should show the action and lead to emotional responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange the play so that the poet sets forth events (showing rather than merely telling), then introduces speech and devices that prepare for the emotional responses. Use ordering to move the audience from demonstration to feeling (pity/fear) before resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate introduction and moderation of names, rituals, and adjunct elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduced names, priesthoods, or ritual devices must be suitable and moderate in the poem; they should serve the poem's species and outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing religious or ritual elements (e.g., temple offices, purifications like Orestes' liberation), ensure they fit the plot and are not gratuitous. Names and institutions should be introduced only when they help the recognition or resolution and kept moderated so as not to overload the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by memory/emotion and by analogy — use carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions effected by memory or emotional reaction (e.g., hearing a song or seeing a writing causes tears) are powerful when credible; analogical recognitions exist but risk error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use memetic or emotive triggers (songs, writings, familiar sights) to provoke recognition when plausible. Avoid faulty analogies or overreliance on hearsay that would produce false recognition or incredibility (the text cites analogical errors leading to mistaken recognition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eloquio (speech) and its elemental units — attend to phonetics, metre and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech is made of elemental parts (syllable, conjunction, separativa, noun, verb, case, sentence). Syllable is a meaningful composite (vowel + consonant) and phonetic shape interacts with meter and meter-placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose diction sensitive to phonetic composition and metrical placement: vary sounds according to lips, place, length, correction, and weight; consider where elements fall in meter (initial, middle, end). Use appropriate speech forms (imperative, prayer, narration, threat, question, answer) fitting the character and situation. Attend to the audible qualities of syllables and consonants for effect; treat speech as part of the art, not accidental ornament.
